title: See It, Hear It: vis and aud
objectives: I can use the roots vis and aud to figure out what new words mean.
I can explain how a word part and a base work together in words like visible and audition.
I can use context clues to understand words about seeing and hearing in a story.
I can write sentences that use words about seeing and hearing correctly.
rationale: Two Latin roots, vis (see) and aud (hear), give students a strategy they can use across school subjects and in science words later on. Putting them in one unit as a contrast set helps students notice that the root carries the core meaning while the ending changes the job of the word (vision, visible, visor; audio, audition, auditorium). Television shows a prefix, a root, and a suffix in one word. The passage is set at a school talent show so every word is used in a natural setting, and it extends the looking words from unit 9 (peek, gaze) and the root work from unit 3.

passage.title: Pia's Audition
paras: Pia stared at the poster on the school wall. Talent Night was only a week away, and the auditions started on Monday. Her goal was to sing in the big auditorium, where hundreds of families would come to watch.

On Monday, Pia walked into the auditorium and saw three teachers sitting in the front row. A bright stage light made her squint, so she borrowed a cap with a visor from her friend Leo. Her vision was clear again, and she felt braver.

Mr. Diaz, the music teacher, helped with the audio system. He tested the microphone and made sure every word would be loud enough to hear. Then he set up a video camera so each performance could be shown later on the classroom television. The audiovisual setup looked complicated, but it worked well.

Pia sang one song. When she finished, the teachers smiled. "Your voice is wonderful," said Mr. Diaz. "Please write your name on the sign-up sheet in big letters so it is visible from across the room." Pia printed her name carefully. Next week, her grandmother would visit to watch her on the stage.

qs.q: In the last paragraph, what does the word "visible" mean?
qs.why: Writing the name in big letters makes it easy to see from across the room.

choices: A try-out where a performer shows what they can do

choices: The stage light was too bright for her eyes.
She wanted to hide from the teachers.
It was raining in the auditorium.
qs.why: The bright stage light made her squint, and then her vision was clear again.

choices: Three teachers sat in the front row.
Mr. Diaz set up a video camera and a classroom television.
qs.why: The camera and television are the equipment that records and shows performances.

qs.q: What is the passage mostly about?
choices: A girl's first try-out for a school show
qs.why: The story follows Pia from the poster to her audition and the plan for Talent Night.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words in two root families, vis (see) and aud (hear), and one word that joins them. The story takes place at a school talent show so they hear every word in a natural setting, and the study task has students break words into parts and name the meaning of each.

notes.va.vision.n: Show vis + ion on the board. Distinguish vision (the ability to see) from the sense of a picture in your mind; this unit teaches the first meaning.
notes.va.video.n: The spelling vid is a variant form of the same Latin see root; do not make students memorize it. Contrast with audio: video is for the eyes, audio is for the ears.
notes.va.visible.adj: Split into vis + -ible, able to be seen. Pair with invisible to show the prefix in- meaning not. Practice with objects that are visible only with a tool.
notes.va.television.n: Break into tele- (far), vis (see), and -ion. Ask: what does it let you do? See far away. The tele- prefix is Greek, the root is Latin.
notes.va.visit.v: Visit comes from a Latin word for going to see, but students do not need to break the word apart. Link to visitor and to the idea of going somewhere to see.
notes.va.audio.n: Audio is built on the Latin hear root. Students often say audio and video mean the same; have them sort examples into two columns.
notes.va.audiovisual.adj: A compound of audio and visual. Ask students to list audiovisual things in the classroom, such as a film or a slideshow with narration.
notes.va.visor.n: Visor is a concrete word, but its history is not clearly about seeing: it comes through an Old French word for face. Teach it as a thing that helps you see and flag the origin for review.
notes.va.audition.n: Split into audit + -ion. The judges listen as well as watch. Students often confuse audition with addition because of the spelling; point to the aud at the front.
notes.va.auditorium.n: Audit + -orium, a place for hearing. Link to audience. Ask where else an audience might sit and what each place is called.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word is audition. I see aud at the front. I know aud means hear, like audio. An audition is when people listen to you perform. That fits the story: the teachers listened to Pia sing.'
